item.title: Experts highlight role of automated assistance system in GJ-21 stealth drone's takeoff and landing aboard Type 076 amphibious assault ship
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07 21:11:00
A simulated animation of a GJ-21 armed reconnaissance stealth drone on board a Type 076 amphibious assault ship. Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News China's first amphibious assault ship equipped with electromagnetic catapults, the Type 076 Sichuan , has made further progress in recent days, with the GJ-21 stealth drone completing its first takeoff and landing operations aboard the vessel. An expert highlighted the significance of automated assistance systems in a report released on Saturday. Another expert noted that, with its unmanned design, the GJ-21 faces no human physical limitations during takeoff and landing and could potentially be adapted for use not only on the Type 076 amphibious assault ship but also on aircraft carriers in the future, including conventionally powered ones. The GJ-21 stealth unmanned aerial vehicle features a tailless flying-wing design with a blended wing-body configuration. It is equipped with an internal weapons bay and internal fuel storage, according to CCTV News. The platform designed to operate it, the Sichuan , is the first hull of the Type 076 amphibious assault ship, which is designed, developed and built independently by China. It has a full-load displacement of more than 40,000 tons. Wei Dongxu, a Chinese military affairs commentator, said that the carrier-based aircraft landings are technically challenging because an aircraft carrier itself is moving at sea. Pilots must constantly adjust the aircraft's altitude, flight angle and speed, while ensuring that its tailhook catches an arresting cable on the carrier's flight deck, according to CCTV News. However, the GJ-21 is uncrewed and operates as an intelligent combat platform. Therefore, it is highly likely that the GJ-21 and the Type 076 amphibious assault ship Sichuan will rely on intelligent and automated assistance systems, Wei added. "For example, through signals, the GJ-21 could autonomously sense the Sichuan's navigation conditions to a certain extent, adjust itself and adapt accordingly, ultimately completing the entire landing sequence efficiently, quickly and precisely," Wei continued, CCTV reported. As the aircraft is unmanned, there is no need to account for the physical stress that pilots would experience during takeoff and landing, Wang Yunfei, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times. Compared with manned aircraft of a smaller size and weight, it can take off and land more quickly, with less stringent requirements for climb and descent angles, and conduct more sorties, he added. On the other hand, Wang noted that UAVs place higher demands on flight control and command systems. During takeoff and landing, they may encounter wind updrafts or downdrafts. Unlike manned aircraft, where pilots can make immediate adjustments, UAVs rely heavily on onboard AI and remote-control systems. The successful takeoff and landing of the GJ-21 on board the Type 076 amphibious assault ship showed that China has reached the world's highest level in terms of drone adaptability on aircraft carrier. Wang also noted that aircraft carriers by conventional means could also adopt this automated takeoff and landing assistance system in the future. "If it works successfully on the Type 076 amphibious assault ship, it should theoretically be possible to adapt it for other aircraft carriers," he said. Once the system has been tested on the Sichuan and sufficient test data has been collected, it could potentially be introduced on other carriers equipped with electromagnetic catapults, he added. "This would expand the range of aircraft operating from our carriers and further enhance their unmanned combat capabilities."

item.title: Australian lobster, wine and goat meat draw crowds at CIIE as exporters eye bigger China market
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07 19:38:00
A view of the Team Australia Pavilion of the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) held in Shanghai on November 7, 2026. Photo: Tu Lei/ Global Times At the Team Australia Pavilion of the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) held in Shanghai, visitors crowded around to sample freshly cooked Australian lobster topped with melted cheese. Marc Anderson, CEO of Geraldton Fishermen's Co-operative, watched the bustling tasting session with a smile from behind the crowd. Nearly two years have passed since China lifted restrictions on Australian lobster imports. Anderson and his team are leveraging the CIIE platform to help Chinese consumers gain deeper insights into Australian rock lobster. “It’s a great opportunity to meet so many people. This helps us build broader brand recognition, which is important for us, and reconnect with our customers here in China,” Anderson told the Global Times on Friday. “We’ve been back in the Chinese market for nearly two years, and the market is growing stronger. We are committed to the Chinese market as part of our broader diversified market strategy,” he said. Anderson said they have around 5,000 tons of lobster and roughly 60 percent of the output may go to China. It takes just eight hours by air to transport the lobsters from waters off Western Australia to Hong Kong, before they are shipped onward to Xiamen, Guangzhou or Shanghai. Anderson’s booth is not the only busy spot. Just a few meters away stands a freezer stocked with frozen Australian goat meat. Miriam Blythe, export manager at Western Meat Exporters Pty Ltd, is attending the CIIE with her company’s products for the first time. “We have whole goat carcasses, as well as pre-cut goat cubes ready for hot pot and home cooking,” she explained to the Global Times when pointing to the freezer on Saturday. Blythe said her company has been exporting Australian goat meat to China for 13 years. China accounts for roughly 10 percent of its sales, yet this marks the firm’s debut at the CIIE. Adam Qiu from Shenhui (Shanghai) Food Co has partnered with Western Meat Exporters Pty Ltd for nine years. He was among those who pushed hard to encourage the Australian exporter to take part in the CIIE. “I told them this is China’s biggest expo. Unlike specialized food fairs, it is a comprehensive event that draws all kinds of visitors,” he told the Global Times. “At the CIIE, we are not merely selling meat. More importantly, we get to showcase the products to the entire Chinese market,” he added. During the pavilion tour, the Global Times saw familiar Australian staples such as beef, wine, milk powder and honey on display, with animated conversations unfolding at the booths. Adjacent to the displays sits a kitchen preparing roasted beef and lobster, and its savory aroma drifts through the air. Ding Youzhen, who oversees the China market at Australia Swan Vintage Pty Ltd, has attended the CIIE for nine consecutive years and is among the expo’s beneficiaries. Swan Vintage runs its own wineries in Australia, exporting roughly two million to three million bottles of wine to China annually for distribution by local Chinese distributors, he told the Global Times. China is the company’s most important global market outside Australia and its largest by sales volume, he said. Occupying more than 1,700 square meters, Australia’s national pavilion hosts a total of 190 Australian firms at this year’s CIIE. They are showcasing Australian packaged food, wine, beverages, dairy, meat, seafood, health food and agricultural products, data from the Australia Trade and Investment Commission (Austrade) showed. Yan Dong, Vice Minister of Commerce, said at the CIIE press conference on October 16 that the exhibition space occupied by Australian enterprises had expanded by 25 percent from last year. “Roughly 30 to 40 of the 190 Australian exhibitors are first-time participants at the CIIE,” John Madew, Senior Trade and Investment Commissioner at Austrade, told the Global Times on Saturday. “We are an export-driven economy, and there will always be new firms with new products wanting to test them in China. The CIIE is best suited for so-called export-ready companies, yet it also welcomes new businesses. You never know until you try. It remains a fantastic window into the diversity and dynamism of the Chinese market,” Madew said. In his view, the expansion of the exhibition area is the result of joint collaboration among different governments and multiple organizations. To help Australian businesses further expand overseas markets, the Australian government has rolled out the Access to New Market Initiative, with support for companies participating in exhibitions in China as a key component of the program, he said.

item.title: China has capacity, willingness to advance global marine biodiversity governance, expert says
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07 17:02:00
Photo: VCG China has both the capacity and willingness to play a bigger role in global marine biodiversity governance, including by supporting developing countries and hosting the Secretariat of the UN treaty on marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement) in Xiamen, an expert told the Global Times on Saturday. The remarks came as a report on China's role in global marine biodiversity governance was released in both Chinese and English on Thursday. China, by helping bridge differences between developed and developing countries, has advanced the conclusion of a landmark agreement in global ocean governance, namely the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction, which entered into force early this year, according to the report released by the China Institute for Marine Affairs under the Ministry of Natural Resources. Chen Xidi, an expert at the China Institute for Marine Affairs under the Ministry of Natural Resources, told the Global Times that a considerable number of countries expect China to play a greater role in implementing the BBNJ Agreement. “China has the capacity and willingness to meet these expectations,” he said. In designing and refining relevant legal arrangements, China has advocated a benefit-sharing mechanism encompassing both monetary and non-monetary benefits to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of developing countries, and supported an integrated approach to biodiversity conservation and the sustainable use of marine resources, said the report. A model of the Jiaolong manned submersible on display at the National Maritime Museum of China in North China's Tianjin Municipality on October 2, 2026. Photo: VCG The report noted that China has made its research platforms accessible to international partners and shared scientific results with them through scientific research expeditions conducted using its deep-sea submersibles such as Jiaolong and Fendouzhe, as well as research vessels like Shenhai Yihao. China has also preserved nearly 60,000 samples of marine microbial resources and established repositories and databases, and offered specialized services to facilitate access to samples and data. The country has also supported developing countries in environmental impact assessment, according to the report. "China has continued to make its marine research expeditions open to international partners, working with foreign experts on joint marine research projects using its advanced vessels and facilities. Under the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development, China has also launched international large-scale scientific programs that bring together scientists from dozens of countries," Chen said. China has also provided assistance to developing countries in Africa and the Pacific region in areas such as seabed surveys and exploration, and marine spatial planning. It has actively opened up and shared marine genetic resources and related information, helping advance international marine scientific research, Chen added. “Through scientific expeditions and surveys in the high seas and international seabed areas, China has also helped expand humanity's understanding of the deep ocean, generating scientific knowledge that can benefit the international community and support global conservation efforts,” he noted. Beyond its efforts in research, China has made substantial efforts to protect marine ecosystems at home. It has designated about 150,000 square kilometers of marine ecological conservation red-line areas, established 353 marine protected areas and implemented 194 marine ecological conservation projects. Notably, China is among the few countries worldwide to have achieved a net increase in mangrove areas, a significant achievement reflecting its progress in domestic marine conservation, Chen explained. The report also highlights China's expanding network of marine cooperation. China has signed marine cooperation agreements with more than 50 countries and international organizations, jointly established over 40 marine research centers and laboratories, and invested about 200 million yuan ($29.96 million) in more than 100 small but impactful marine cooperation projects. It has also organized more than 300 training courses in marine science, technology and management, benefiting over 6,000 young researchers and officials from developing countries. China's application to host the BBNJ Secretariat in Xiamen is another part of these efforts. The report notes that by applying to host the Secretariat, the country has undertaken further international responsibilities to address the absence of headquarters of UN ocean-related bodies in Asia and provide a platform for China to contribute to the agreement's implementation. The report highlights the milestone significance of the BBNJ Agreement for global ocean governance and showcases China's significant contributions to its adoption and implementation, experts said.

item.title: One year on, Takaichi's erroneous remark remains uncorrected, and Japan's fangs are growing back
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07 15:54:00
Japan Illustration: Liu Rui/GT A year ago, on November 7, 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made an erroneous remark on the Taiwan question in the Diet, planting a political time bomb in China-Japan relations that has yet to be defused. She claimed that a so-called "Taiwan contingency" could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan. The implication was unmistakable: Tokyo no longer regards the Taiwan question as a matter of Chinese sovereignty. Tokyo was signaling that it might use force to intervene under the guise of defending its own national security. Three days later, she went on to say, "I gave a somewhat concrete answer while considering the worst-case scenario," declining to backtrack on her remarks. A year on, the erroneous words still stand - as does the refusal to correct them. On Friday, a Japanese journalist asked at a regular press conference held by China's Foreign Ministry what China's position was on the current and future China-Japan relations, noting that Saturday marked one year since Takaichi's remarks on Taiwan. The question itself is almost absurd. Having refused to correct a remark that strikes at the foundations of bilateral ties, Japan now wonders when China will be willing to resume normal relations. There is a fundamental principle that Tokyo seems unwilling to grasp: A country cannot provoke its neighbor and then expect to carry on as if nothing has happened. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun left little room for ambiguity. He said the current serious difficulties in China-Japan relations are entirely the responsibility of the Japanese side. It stems from the erroneous remarks made by the Japanese leader a year ago regarding Taiwan, which blatantly signaled a potential military intervention in the Taiwan question, challenged China's national sovereignty, and undermined the political foundation of China-Japan relations. Regrettably, one year on, the Japanese authorities have not moved at all. They've been evading the issue and yet to demonstrate any sincerity or take any action to reflect upon and correct the wrongdoings. Guo added that "our position on China-Japan relations has been consistent. We wish to reiterate that for the Japanese side, the pressing priority is to correct the erroneous words and deeds on the Taiwan question, adopt a correct attitude on historical issues, and form an objective and rational perception on China." However, in the past year, Japan has not only failed to correct that erroneous remark but has also pressed ahead on other fronts. While describing China as its so-called "greatest strategic challenge," it has rapidly increased military spending, pursued long-range strike capabilities, and accelerated programs involving unmanned systems, cyber, and space. A nation that once brought deep suffering to Asia through its war of aggression is now, in the name of a so-called changing security environment, expanding the reach of its military activities once more. For China, this is not a theoretical debate about security. It is a reopening of painful historical memory. The legacy of WWII across Asia is too painful to be brushed aside: war, massacres, human experimentation, systematic plunder and brutal abuse. Yet the former aggressor is now rearming while flipping the narrative, portraying the past victim as today's threat. Its prime minister has gone further, tying the Taiwan Straits to Japan's national survival. The recent discussion of possible exceptions to Japan' s Three Non-Nuclear Principles has exposed the country's ambition more plainly. The principles stipulate that the country will not possess or produce nuclear weapons, or permit their introduction into the country. Yet the Takaichi government aims to revise the National Security Strategy by year's end to allow nuclear weapons to be brought into the country in an emergency. Japan is steadily testing how far it can move beyond the constraints that have defined its postwar role. The series of words and deeds have already cracked the shell of Japan's "exclusively defense-oriented" posture. A country that repeatedly proclaims its commitment to peace is now demonstrating, through its own actions, precisely why the postwar order imposed constraints on Japanese militarism in the first place. There is no such bargain. Japan cannot strike at China's core interests and still expect normal relations. It cannot discard postwar military limits and demand that its neighbors believe its peaceful intent. Nor can it evade its history of aggression while expecting those it once harmed to accept its remilitarization. What Japan is making increasingly clear to the rest of Asia is that the return of the fangs begins with the return of the camouflage. The language is carefully chosen: "defense," "worst-case scenario," "survival-threatening situation." These are the excuses Japan is using to beef up its military muscle in ways that would once have been politically unthinkable. Step by step, it is building a rationale - for itself and for others - for why it should once again be able to bare its fangs and strike. A year ago, Takaichi tested China's red line. Today, Japan is testing the postwar order itself. The political time bomb planted then remains undetonated. Those responsible have made no effort to defuse it. Instead, Japan's military machinery is gathering speed. The postwar restraints are being tested. The fangs are growing back.

item.title: China, US top trade officials hold video call as Beijing raises serious concerns over restrictions; Washington urged to honor leaders' consensus
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07 14:00:00
An aerial image shows cargo shipping containers and cranes as cargo containers sit stacked on freight trains at the Port of Long Beach in Long Beach, California on April 10, 2025. Photo: VCG The lead officials for China-US economic and trade affairs held a video call on Friday, focusing on implementing the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and the outcomes of bilateral economic and trade consultations, Xinhua News Agency reported on Saturday. During the call, the Chinese side expressed serious concerns over recent US economic and trade restrictions against China. A Chinese expert noted that the latest dialogue showed that both sides still have an incentive to stabilize trade relations despite persistent friction, but Washington needs to take concrete steps to uphold the consensus reached by the two leaders. Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, also China's lead person for China-US economic and trade affairs, held a video call on Friday with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, Xinhua reported. The two sides held candid, in-depth, and constructive exchanges on implementing the important consensus reached between the two heads of state at their meetings in Beijing and Washington and the outcomes of economic and trade consultations, and on key economic and trade issues of mutual concern, Xinhua said. Both sides agreed that under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, they would further leverage the China-US economic and trade consultation mechanism, continuously strengthen cooperation and properly manage differences so as to promote the stable and positive development of China-US economic and trade relations, and contribute to building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, according to Xinhua. Despite persistent friction, the latest dialogue showed that both China and the US still have a strong incentive to stabilize bilateral trade relations, providing an important basis for further engagement through the economic and trade consultation mechanism, Li Yong, a senior research fellow at the China Association of International Trade, told the Global Times on Saturday. "By maintaining high-level dialogue, both sides are showing a continued willingness to resolve differences and follow through on the consensus reached by their leaders," Li said, noting that such engagement is crucial to keeping bilateral trade relations stable. The latest video call came as the two countries were working to implement the outcomes of the eighth round of their economic and trade consultations in New York and Washington from September 20 to 23. During September's consultations, China and the US reached a series of agreements on tariff reductions, trade and investment mechanisms, and the extension of existing trade arrangements. Yet Washington has since imposed or proposed new restrictions on Chinese businesses, including measures involving technology firms, outbound investment and biotechnology. The latest case came on Thursday, when the US State Department imposed new Cuba-related sanctions, including on two Chinese companies accused of supplying electronic and security equipment to the Cuban military. China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) on Saturday firmly opposed the move, saying the US has imposed unilateral sanctions on Chinese companies on the grounds of their involvement with a third party, in violation of international law and basic norms of international relations. MOFCOM said the US had recently intensified sanctions and pressure on China, rapidly rolling out a series of discriminatory and restrictive measures. These measures have seriously harmed the rights and interests of Chinese companies, run counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, and undermined the stability of China-US economic and trade relations. On Friday, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that China firmly opposes illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or lack UN Security Council authorization, as well as the so-called "long-arm jurisdiction." He reaffirmed China's opposition to US attempts to disrupt and sabotage China-Cuba cooperation and said China would take all necessary measures to protect Chinese companies' legitimate rights and interests. Li said Washington's practice of dragging Chinese companies into geopolitical disputes involving third countries and imposing sanctions through so-called "long-arm jurisdiction" lacked justification. “The US continues to create problems, though this has not derailed bilateral economic and trade ties. Both sides are still making efforts to keep the relationship on a normal track,” Li said. However, he stressed that these restrictive measures have caused significant harm to current China-US economic and trade relations. “The US has long championed free trade and fair treatment, but its economic policies toward China remain heavily influenced by politicization and an overstretched concept of national security,” Li added. By contrast, China has remained rational and restrained in its response to unjustified US restrictions, and has sought to manage differences through established economic and trade consultation and dispute-resolution mechanisms rather than escalating tensions, according to the expert. Under the September agreements, the two sides plan to hold another AI dialogue by the end of November and their agricultural working group's first meeting by the end of 2026. They also agreed to extend the Kuala Lumpur economic and trade consultations arrangement until January 10, 2027, while continuing discussions toward a mutually agreed solution, according to the MOFCOM’s website. Li said China remained committed to advancing cooperation through mechanisms such as the trade and investment councils. "Both sides should approach economic and trade cooperation from the perspective of making the pie bigger," he said. Washington, for its part, needs to move beyond politicizing trade and overstating national security concerns, and focus on implementing the consensus reached by the two countries’ leaders and building stable economic ties.

item.title: From Yiwu to Africa: How China's market opening is creating new opportunities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07 08:32:00
Picture of the 15th meeting of the China-Africa Think Tank Forum At the bustling Yiwu International Trade Market in East China’s Zhejiang Province, visitors from African countries including Kenya, Malawi, Zimbabwe and Rwanda moved from stall to stall, peppering merchants with questions about how their products were made, how much they cost to produce, how profitable they were and how far their reach extended across global markets. The visitors were equally captivated by displays of Chinese technological innovation, from robots dancing to music to AI-powered glasses that allow users to answer phone calls and take photographs without reaching for their smartphones. “I’ve traveled around the world, but I’ve never been to a place quite like the Yiwu International Trade Market. It’s incredibly innovative. You saw me dancing with the robots and even talking to them — something I could hardly have imagined,” George W. Chaima, country director of New Restoration Plan, a think tank in Malawi, told the Global Times. “China is not just busy developing new technologies; it is also building nations, building bridges and bringing the world together through development and mutual cooperation. I think that is exactly what the world is missing,” said Chaima. Chaima and other guests are part of the participants of this year’s meeting of the China-Africa Think Tanks Forum which was opened in Yiwu on Friday. At this forum, the Think Tank Action Declaration on Advancing Modernization in the Global South Through China-Africa Cooperation, and China-Africa Consensus on Mutual Learning Between Civilizations were released. Speaking at the opening ceremony, Oumar Demba Ba, chief diplomat adviser to the president of Senegal, said that China and Africa have consistently worked together in a spirit of peace and mutual respect. Against a backdrop of rising unilateralism and trade protectionism, he spoke highly of China's landmark decision to grant zero-tariff treatment to African countries with which it has diplomatic relations. He stressed that Africa should strengthen its own think tanks and develop an independent African narrative to challenge entrenched stereotypes and prejudices, while advancing China-Africa cooperation to a higher level and ensuring that its progress becomes irreversible. In May, China expanded its zero-tariff treatment to cover all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties, creating new opportunities for Africa to boost exports and industrialization amid the global headwinds of protectionism. China had already scrapped tariffs on 100 percent of tariff lines for 33 least developed countries (LDCs) in Africa since Dec. 1, 2024. The new zero-tariff policy will benefit the relatively better-off countries such as Kenya, Egypt and Nigeria, according to Xinhua News Agency. Under the new arrangement, zero tariffs will apply to the 20 African non-LDCs in the form of a preferential tariff rate for two years, during which China will continue to promote the signing of the China-Africa Economic Partnership for Shared Development agreement with relevant African countries. Officials said the agreement will fix zero tariffs as a long-term institutional arrangement. Sylvia Sinkari, a consultant with China Europe International Business School Africa, said China's emphasis is increasingly on encouraging African countries to add value to their products before exporting them. “This is an export-led approach that creates opportunities for African economies to move beyond raw commodity exports and develop more competitive, value-added products. China is also working to strengthen the capacities of African countries so that they can process and manufacture products that meet the requirements of the Chinese market,” said Sinkari. China's comprehensive zero-tariff treatment toward African countries has delivered notable results, with China's imports from African countries rising 21.6 percent year-on-year from May to September this year. The policy has not only benefited people's livelihoods but is also expected to provide a strong boost to Africa's industrialization, Liu Yuxi, Ambassador for the Affairs of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, said at the opening ceremony. For Sylvia, the sprawling markets of Yiwu offer more than a glimpse into China's manufacturing prowess. They also provide a potential model for African businesses seeking to move beyond exporting raw materials and become more competitive in global markets. "China has given us the market access," she said, stressing that African governments and businesses must now seize the opportunity to develop their manufacturing capabilities and export more value-added products. Drawing on her experience in supply chain management, Sylvia described Yiwu as a place where African entrepreneurs could work with Chinese manufacturers to turn business ideas into products, from design and packaging to meeting international standards. "You sit with your Chinese partners, you co-create this, and then you sell to the world," she said.

item.title: After US Democrats' midterm win, Taiwan authorities scramble for cracks in new Congress' door: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 23:53:00
Illustration: Liu Rui/GT The DPP authorities fancy that their intensive networking and hedging of bets following the US midterm elections demonstrate sophisticated "political wisdom." Little do they realize that such behavior is not only laughable but also extremely dangerous in the arena of international politics. Such shortsighted political maneuvering can do nothing to change the fate of the DPP authorities as a mere pawn. The US midterm elections have barely concluded, yet some on the island of Taiwan are already anxious. Within just a few days, think tanks and "external affairs" institutions in Taipei sprang into action, organizing one seminar and media interview after another. Green camp politicians and so-called "strategic scholars" rushed to assess the shifting balance of power in the new US Congress, calculating how to establish ties with the incoming powerbrokers in both the House and the Senate as quickly as possible. They are eager to submit their political "pledges of allegiance" through various lobbying channels, even if all they can secure is an empty promise of "support for Taiwan." This kind of restless anxiety - both fearful and impatient - is less a sign of so-called "agile response in external strategy" than a full exposure of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities' deeply opportunistic and politically parasitic nature. This kind of restlessness fully exposes the true nature of certain politicians on the island as "political chameleons." In the political vocabulary of the DPP authorities, there are no inviolable principles, let alone any steadfast convictions. All they represent is nothing but naked opportunism. Whenever the political winds shift in Washington, these self-proclaimed far-sighted strategists are quick to change course and switch their positions. They know how to play both sides of the aisle and pull strings across the US political spectrum. When the Democrats are in power, they talk about "progressive values," "green transition" and "human rights alliances." When Republicans take control, they overnight adopt a "hardline anti-China posture" and present themselves as staunch advocates of "fully preparing for war." No sooner had the midterm elections concluded than think tanks on the island rushed to compile profiles of newly elected members of the House and the Senate, scheming to redesign their lobbying strategies. In their eyes, regardless of Washington's political ideology or policy agenda, as long as it can provide a fig leaf for the DPP's "Taiwan independence" separatist fantasies, they are willing to bend over backwards to please their American patrons, with little regard for their own dignity. DPP politicians constantly proclaim that "the relations between the US and the Taiwan region are rock-solid" and that the two sides "share democratic values." Yet beneath this polished rhetoric lies a sordid record of naked self-interest. In their dealings with Washington, the DPP authorities go out of their way to flatter their American patrons, willingly putting the foundation of industries vital to the livelihoods of Taiwan residents on the negotiating table. They have effectively handed over Taiwan region's core semiconductor assets as a package, allowing them to be relocated overseas and gradually hollowing out the island's industrial base. Meanwhile, they are also signing off on massive purchases of obsolete military equipment at exorbitant prices, with delivery dates nowhere in sight, squandering Taiwan regional taxpayers' money on Washington's lobbying and military-industrial interest groups. Behind the scenes, their every calculation is driven by the DPP's dream of "staying in power." They seem to imagine that a few cheap declarations of loyalty will bind the US firmly onto their narrow and dangerous "anti-China" bandwagon, while harboring ulterior motives to shirk responsibility and shift the blame whenever Washington actually demands that they pay the price. Such shortsighted political maneuvering can do nothing to change the fate of the DPP authorities as a mere pawn. How can a political party willing to sell out national dignity and cultural roots possibly possess political foresight? The DPP authorities fancy that their intensive networking and hedging of bets following the US midterm elections demonstrate sophisticated "political wisdom." Little do they realize that such behavior is not only laughable but also extremely dangerous in the arena of international politics. Politics requires principles, and international engagement demands credibility. The DPP authorities lack any strategic resolve in their external dealings, while on the island, they know only how to foment confrontation and division. Every frantic maneuver and attempt to test the waters in response to shifts in American political power will not alter in the slightest the historical trend that both sides of the Taiwan Straits belong to one China and that China will inevitably achieve reunification. Instead, they are pushing Taiwan region, step by step, toward an abyss of irreversible disaster. When a pawn becomes so absorbed in its role that it imagines it can dictate the course of the game, the stage is often set for being ruthlessly abandoned. In the harsh reality of great-power competition, history has long established the ultimate fate of opportunists who lack the backing of real strength, have abandoned political integrity, and survive entirely through delusional dependence on others. The more the DPP authorities display their almost neurotic anxiety and fickleness, the more they expose their profound sense of insecurity. The world can clearly see through this desperate political farce unfolding on the island. No matter how frequently seminars are held in Taiwan, or how meticulously DPP lobbyists prepare their briefing materials, none of it can conceal their despicable nature as self-serving opportunists who sacrifice principles for personal gain. The tide of history cannot be stopped by a handful of power-hungry politicians. In the face of the Chinese nation's determined march toward great rejuvenation, all the frantic maneuvers and delusional dreams of those who seek "'Taiwan independence' by relying on the US" and sell themselves out for personal gain will ultimately be crushed beneath the relentlessly advancing wheels of history.

item.title: AI helps track tigers, gibbons and elephants to turn sightings into protection in China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 23:21:00
A display showcases the AI-powered wildlife monitoring system used in Changchun, Northeast China's Jilin Province. Photo: Shan Jie/Global Times A wild Siberian tiger does not pose for an identification photograph. It may pass a forest camera sideways, turn its back or leave only its head in view. For a computer trying to establish which tiger has appeared, those incomplete glimpses present a challenge. Unlike human faces, the markings of endangered wild animals come with relatively few examples from which an algorithm can learn, Hu Xinyu, a senior manager at Jishi Media, which provides technical support for Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park's wildlife monitoring system, told the Global Times. Yet these brief encounters are becoming increasingly useful. At Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, connected cameras and AI-assisted analysis help staff link an animal's appearance to its previous sightings, follow its movements and identify possible risks near villages. Across China, similar approaches are extending from forest images to rainforest sounds. The practical question is how to turn these records into knowledge that helps people protect wildlife. Recognizing the unseen The first task is getting information out of the forest. At Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, a communications network operating in the 700 MHz frequency band connects cameras across mountainous terrain. Hu said footage can reach monitoring centers within about a minute of capture, allowing staff to examine activity without waiting for someone to retrieve a memory card. AI then helps sort the incoming material. But identifying a tiger in an image and deciding exactly which tiger it is are different tasks. According to Hu, the system's species recognition accuracy exceeds 90 percent, while individual identification accuracy for some species, including Siberian tigers and Amur leopards, exceeds 80 percent. Researchers still need to review uncertain matches. The distinction matters. Recognizing that a tiger has crossed a camera's field of view records its presence. Matching it to previous images allows researchers to assemble a history: where it travels, which areas it repeatedly visits and whether it appears with cubs. The park's monitoring platform associates identification numbers with images recorded at different locations. Stripes and spots provide distinguishing features, while repeated observations help staff trace dispersing youngsters and breeding families. For rare animals, however, collecting enough suitable examples remains difficult. An animal partly hidden by vegetation or photographed from an unfamiliar angle may offer few usable features. Hu said the team continues working with research institutions to improve identification. In Hainan's tropical rainforests, researchers have been examining another identifying feature: the voice. A gibbon moves through the forest in the Wuliang Mountains in Pu'er, Southwest China's Yunnan Province, on August 3, 2026. Photo: VCG Hainan gibbons spend much of their lives high in the trees, making direct observation difficult. Their calls offer a way to gather information when their bodies remain hidden. A study published in Scientia Silvae Sinicae in 2023 tested whether neural networks could distinguish male Hainan gibbons using spectrograms, visual representations of their calls. Working with recordings from seven males, researchers reported classification accuracy of 95.04 percent for the better-performing model. The result demonstrated a method for distinguishing those individuals. The example shows why wildlife monitoring requires methods adapted to each species. A camera may capture a tiger's markings; a recorder may capture a gibbon that cannot be seen. Both still depend on carefully collected and checked reference data. Experience with snow leopards also illustrates the continuing role of people. Researchers involved in a large-scale Sanjiangyuan survey described using AI to help remove empty camera images and classify animals. Identifying individual snow leopards still relied mainly on people comparing markings, with two observers checking their conclusions independently, according to the National Forestry and Grassland Administration. These systems reduce the burden of searching through records. But establishing what those records mean for a population requires further work, including field observations and ecological analysis. Turning data into protection Knowing where an animal has appeared can also help people decide where to avoid it. In Southwest China's Yunnan Province, Asian elephant monitoring combines infrared cameras, drones and AI image recognition to map elephant activity. It was reported that staff in Xishuangbanna were using these tools to produce activity heat maps, bringing observations from different locations together on a monitoring platform. The information becomes useful through the people and communication channels connected to it. Yunnan's forestry and grassland authorities told the Global Times in a previous interview that professional elephant protection teams carry out routine monitoring and issue warnings to nearby communities through WeChat, text messages and smart broadcasting systems, reminding residents to avoid elephants. AI is also being used to support the captive breeding of Yangtze finless porpoises. In Wuhan, Central China's Hubei Province, researchers have introduced an intelligent behavior monitoring system to follow interactions between mothers and calves, adding detailed observations to the work of animal carers. The system analyzes video to recognize several important mother-calf swimming positions and surfacing behavior. Researchers can use the resulting records to track nursing frequency and duration, assembling observations into standardized growth records for young porpoises. Bawangling National Nature Reserve in South China's Hainan Province provides a forest habitat for Hainan gibbons. Photo: VCG Previously, monitoring required staff to work around the clock in four shifts. Fatigue during overnight observation could affect data quality. The new system helps researchers organize observations more systematically and devote more time to breeding research. The application offers another route from images to conservation: repeated observations of how a calf swims and feeds become records that researchers can review, compare and use in caring for the animal. At the tiger and leopard park, staff similarly use monitoring information to warn communities when large predators approach settlements. Recent activity records also help rangers plan their routes, giving animals space while maintaining patrols. The forest images have another use beyond management. They provide material through which people far from wildlife habitats can learn about the animals living there. During a visit to Jishi Media in Changchun, Northeast China's Jilin Province, production staff described a familiar difficulty in wildlife filmmaking: a camera may record a remarkable moment without capturing enough material to explain an animal's wider life. A representative involved in ecological filmmaking told the Global Times that obtaining continuous footage of wild tigers, including feeding behavior, was difficult. The team draws on monitoring images and documentary materials, combining real footage with AI-generated sequences to present aspects of animal life that are hard to film. The approach is being explored in the documentary project Huxiao Gongsheng (Living with Tigers), which uses AI-generated content to visualize scenes beyond the reach of conventional filming. For the production team, AI offers a way to explain animal behavior that is difficult to capture continuously in the wild. The representative said real monitoring footage and documentary materials provide the basis for the storytelling, while generated sequences help illustrate feeding behavior and food-chain relationships. The team hopes this combination will help audiences understand both the animals' lives and the protection work surrounding them. Stories about tigers entering villages, for example, can also explain how wildlife-damage insurance compensates farmers for livestock losses, showing what coexistence involves for people living near their habitats. Back in the forest, the tiger may still give the camera only a fleeting view. The work continues after it has disappeared from the frame.

item.title: China 'isn't buying' Nvidia chips. Why are some Americans so rattled?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 19:50:00
Nvidia H200 chip Photo: VCG Reuters recently cited "people familiar with the matter" as saying that about 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips piled up in Hong Kong awaiting shipment to the Chinese mainland because they have not been approved for release by the Chinese side. Although neither the Chinese government nor the US government nor Nvidia has confirmed the report, it has already sent some Americans into a tizzy. Some US think tank experts said they find it "bit of a puzzle" why China is being so cautious about Nvidia, while certain media outlets claimed that China is "restricting itself." Judging from the reactions of some people in the US, it seems they have forgotten who was the first to impose sanctions. In 2022, Washington imposed export controls on advanced chips destined for China under the pretext of "national security," immediately placing Nvidia's most advanced chips on the list of products banned from sale to China. These restrictions have since been tightened layer upon layer. Today, not only have affiliates and overseas subsidiaries of restricted Chinese companies been brought under the controls, but alternative routes for accessing advanced computing power through overseas cloud rental arrangements have also come under pressure. Some US politicians have even openly insisted that China must not be given any breathing room, arguing that even chips with reduced processing power should be kept out of its hands. So why is it that some Americans get rattled when China buys Nvidia chips, yet get equally rattled when China chooses not to buy them? Nvidia once held an overwhelmingly dominant position in China's AI chip market. However, successive rounds of US export controls have directly slashed its market share in China to around 30 percent of its previous level. Washington's decision to ease export licensing restrictions on H200 chips for China is essentially an attempt to find buyers for products that have already rolled off the production line but now lag two generations behind the most advanced chips. Yet the Chinese market has not rushed to buy them on the scale Washington anticipated. With large quantities of chips stuck in the distribution pipeline, inventory and revenue pressures are naturally mounting for the companies concerned. US institutions that had hoped to use sales of crippled versions of chips to China to help bankroll domestic semiconductor reshoring efforts are understandably finding it difficult to remain calm. There is a deeper strategic calculation behind this thinking among some in the US: By selling China relatively outdated chips, the US hopes to keep Chinese companies locked into the existing technology ecosystem, slow the development and iteration of China's homegrown chips, and preserve a stable technological gap between the two countries. They apparently assumed that a slight loosening of restrictions would trigger a buying spree in China. But the Chinese market today is no longer at a stage where it must buy whatever the US decides to make available. When procuring chips, companies must first consider long-term supply stability, the sustainability of technological roadmaps, and the security and controllability of supply chains. The actions taken by some in the US over the past several years have fundamentally changed the way Chinese companies make purchasing decisions. To expect them to disregard these risks and resume large-scale purchases is simply contrary to the most basic principles of commercial logic. Ultimately, it is not the Chinese market that is anxious now. The development of China's computing power industry in recent years has demonstrated that an independent technological path can provide sufficient computing capacity to sustain industrial growth. Rather than repeatedly urging China to buy American chips, some in the US would do well to acknowledge a basic reality: The global semiconductor landscape has changed. Any attempt to use export controls to lock other countries out of technological progress will ultimately come back to haunt those imposing the restrictions.

item.title: After 15 years of searching, Mauritian scholar's dream comes true
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 23:04:00
Seesaghur and Wu exchange gifts. Photo: Xinmin Evening News Hans Seesaghur, a scholar from Mauritius, had been looking for a Shanghai citizen named Wu Xinmin for 15 years. His dream finally came true. On November 2, Seesaghur and Wu Xinmin met face to face in Shanghai. In 2011, while pursuing his postgraduate studies at Wuhan University, Central China's Hubei Province, Seesaghur conducted research on the history of exchanges between China and Mauritius. During the process, Seesaghur, born in the 1980s, discovered that a Chinese table tennis delegation had visited Mauritius in 1972. In a news archive of the People's Daily, Seesaghur read Wu's name. However, despite years of searching, he was unable to contact Wu. In 2021, Seesaghur read an exclusive interview by the Xinmin Evening News with Wu. After contacting the media outlet, Seesaghur was able to meet Wu. Then, Wu was 23 years old and the captain of the Shanghai table tennis team. In 1972, Wu and Team China traveled to five African countries - Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Mauritius and Uganda - for a total of 68 friendly games. During their meeting, Wu shared with Seesaghur the materials of visiting itinerary, press clippings, and old photographs. Seesaghur is working on a book project, featuring the diplomatic history of Mauritius since its independence, with China-Mauritius relations serving as one of the key topics. Global Times
